title: Care work overload and intimate partner violence against women: the case of Mexico
abstract: This article examines the association between unpaid care work overload and intimate partner violence (IPV) against women in Mexico. Using microdata from the 2021 National Survey on the Dynamics of Household Relationships, the study conceptualises care overload as a gendered structural source of economic and time-related vulnerability that may increase women’s exposure to violence within intimate relationships. The empirical strategy combines probit models with a propensity score matching (PSM) approach to compare women facing high unpaid care burdens with observationally similar women with lower care responsibilities. The PSM strategy improves comparability between treated and control groups by balancing a wide set of observable sociodemographic, household and economic characteristics. The results show that women experiencing unpaid care work overload exhibit a significantly higher probability of IPV, even after accounting for observable confounders. These estimates are consistent in sign but smaller in magnitude than those obtained from baseline probit models. The findings contribute to the literature on gender, care economies and violence by providing robust evidence from a middle-income country using quasi-experimental techniques. From a policy perspective, the results highlight the importance of integrating care policies into strategies aimed at preventing gender-based violence.
